edges.effect_quant: In a crossover breakfast-meal study, increasing the ascorbic-acid to iron molar ratio from 0.6:1 to 1.6:1 raised geometric mean iron absorption from 5.1% to 8.2% (P < 0.01).
edges.population: healthy children and adults consuming non-heme iron with meals
edges.mechanism: Vitamin C reduces ferric to ferrous iron and forms soluble chelates that help non-heme iron remain absorbable in the presence of meal inhibitors. Its effect is strongest in single-meal settings with inhibitor-rich foods and becomes smaller when averaged across a complete diet.
edges.summary: Vitamin C taken with a meal is one of the best established enhancers of non-heme iron absorption, although the size of the effect depends on the meal context. Controlled feeding studies show clear absorption gains in test meals, while whole-diet data suggest the benefit is real but less dramatic than simplified single-meal experiments imply.
edges.caveats: The enhancement is not equally strong across all dietary patterns and iron forms, and long-term vitamin C supplementation does not always translate into a large iron-status effect. This edge is therefore about meal-level absorption facilitation rather than a guarantee of improved body iron stores in every setting.

evidence.citation: Davidsson L et al 2001 Am J Clin Nutr
evidence.notes: Improving iron absorption from a Peruvian school breakfast meal by adding ascorbic acid or Na2EDTA.

evidence.citation: Cook JD et al 2001 Am J Clin Nutr
evidence.notes: Effect of ascorbic acid intake on nonheme-iron absorption from a complete diet.
